Limestone & Lime Chemistry

Lime is one of the most important and versatile materials — a foundation of construction, agriculture, water treatment, and chemistry. Understanding limestone geology and the lime process enables you to produce lime and use it effectively.

Limestone Geology and Identification

Limestone Composition

Primary mineral: Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)

Common rock types:

  • Limestone: >50% CaCO₃; precipitated from seawater
  • Chalk: White, soft limestone; fossil plankton
  • Marble: Metamorphosed limestone; crystalline
  • Shell limestone: Shells compressed and cemented

Identifying Limestone

Field tests:

Test Result Indicates
Hardness Scratches easily with knife Soft carbonate (limestone or chalk)
Acid test Fizzes with HCl or vinegar Carbonate present; likely CaCO₃
Color White, gray, tan, rarely colored Purity (white = pure; color = impurities)
Grain Visible shells, crystalline, fine Rock type variation
Weight Heavy (denser than sandstone) Density consistent with carbonate

Purity assessment:

  • Pure limestone: White, no acid-resistant residue (>95% CaCO₃)
  • Silica content: Leaves fine sand residue after acid test (silica doesn't react with acid)
  • Clay content: Makes muddy suspension in acid (clay particles suspend)
  • Iron content: Reddish/brown tint, red residue after acid

Suitable Limestone for Lime Production

Best sources:

  • High-purity limestone (>90% CaCO₃)
  • Low silica (minimal acid-insoluble residue)
  • Low clay
  • Easy to mine/quarry

Marginal sources:

  • Impure limestone (70–90% CaCO₃) — produces lime with filler (sand, clay)
  • Still usable; resulting lime is somewhat weaker but acceptable
  • Impurities become part of mortar/plaster (filler)

Unsuitable:

  • Dolomite (MgCO₃·CaCO₃): Different chemistry; requires different firing
  • Shale, clay, sandstone: Not carbonates

Calcination: Converting Limestone to Lime

Heating limestone to high temperature decomposes it to lime (CaO) and CO₂.

Chemistry

Thermal decomposition:

  • Limestone (CaCO₃) + heat → Quicklime (CaO) + Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
  • Temperature: 825°C (1517°F) minimum; 900–1100°C typical
  • Above 1200°C: Quicklime begins to sintering (hardening, less reactive)

Equilibrium considerations:

  • Reaction reverses at high temperature if CO₂ not removed
  • Modern kilns draw out CO₂ gas; medieval kilns relied on heat + oxygen flow

Historical Lime Kilns

Clamp kiln (simplest):

  1. Stack limestone blocks in dome shape
  2. Fuel wood at base (or mixed with limestone)
  3. Light fire; maintain for hours to days
  4. Cool slowly
  5. Unstack and retrieve quicklime

Limitations: Uneven heating; long process; significant fuel use

Pit kiln (improved):

  • Limestone stacked in pit with fuel
  • Similar principle; better heat retention

Kiln (traditional permanent):

Updraft kiln (common medieval design):

  1. Stone base with central arch opening
  2. Fuel (wood, coal) burned in lower chamber
  3. Limestone loaded from top
  4. Hot gases rise through limestone
  5. CO₂ escapes; quicklime drops to bottom
  6. Ash/residue cleaned out periodically

Efficiency: Better than clamp; 5–10 tons per day possible with good management

Temperature management:

  • Observe limestone blocks: Should turn white (calcined) from bottom upward
  • If any gray remains: Undercalcined; back into kiln
  • If red/brown: Overcalcined (sintering); less reactive
  • Goal: Pure white, friable chunks

Modern Kiln Construction (DIY)

For small-scale production (backyard level):

  1. Drum kiln: Vertical steel drum, fuel underneath

    • Insulate exterior (brick, clay)
    • Limestone inside; heat from below
    • 2–3 tons capacity; several hours

  2. Rocket stove kiln: Efficient wood burning

    • Use rocket mass heater design
    • Channel hot gases through limestone chamber
    • More fuel-efficient than clamp kiln

  3. Trench kiln: Underground fire, limestone above

    • Dig pit; build fire at bottom
    • Cover with grate or arch
    • Limestone on top; insulate
    • Simplest if you have fuel wood and patience

Fuel options:

  • Wood (traditional, most accessible)
  • Coal (burns hotter; more efficient)
  • Oil, gas (modern; requires infrastructure)

Lime Slaking (Quicklime to Slaked Lime)

Converting caustic quicklime (CaO) to slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂) and making it safe to handle.

The Slaking Reaction

Chemistry:

  • Quicklime (CaO) + water → Slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂) + Heat
  • Reaction is exothermic (very hot!)
  • Temperature rises to boiling; water can steam violently

Stoichiometry:

  • 1 kg quicklime requires ~0.3 kg water (roughly)
  • Excess water = hydrated slurry (suspension)
  • Insufficient water = lumps of unslaked material

Traditional Slaking Process

Procedure (CAUTION: Very hot!):

  1. Collect quicklime chunks from kiln (cooled to safe touch)
  2. Place in large container (concrete mixer, stone trough)
  3. Add water slowly (not all at once!)
  4. Stand back (can splash; extremely hot)
  5. Stir with hoe or stick (avoid splashing)
  6. Add more water gradually until workable consistency
  7. Let cool; allow to settle
  8. Skim white slurry on top (slaked lime)
  9. Strain to remove impurities (ash, unburned limestone)

Result: Slaked lime putty or slurry, ready for use

Forms of Slaked Lime

Hydrated lime (powder):

  • Heat slaked slurry to remove water (traditional: slow drying)
  • Grind to powder
  • Stores dry indefinitely
  • Rehydrate by adding water before use

Lime putty (thick slurry):

  • Less water removed; thick paste remains
  • Traditional form for mortars/plasters
  • Stores in sealed containers; can age (improves over time)
  • High-quality traditional mortars use aged putty (months to years)

Milk of lime (thin slurry):

  • Dilute slaked lime with water
  • Used for limewash, coating applications
  • Separates on standing (solids sink); re-stir before use

Hydraulic vs Non-Hydraulic Lime

The presence of silicates determines setting mechanism and properties.

Non-Hydraulic Lime (Pure)

Composition: Calcium hydroxide only (no silicates)

Setting mechanism:

  • Absorbs CO₂ from air
  • Converts: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ (calcite)
  • Very slow (months to years for thick mortars)
  • Dependent on air contact and drying

Properties:

  • Very flexible (accommodates movement)
  • Breathable (allows water vapor transmission)
  • Soft surface (easily repointed)
  • Poor underwater use (slow hardening)

Uses:

  • Interior plasters
  • Historic masonry (flexible, compatible)
  • Limewash
  • Stucco (exterior, but not water-immersed)

Hydraulic Lime (Contains Silicates)

Composition: Calcium hydroxide + silicates (from clay in limestone)

Setting mechanism:

  • Two processes: Hydration (chemical with silicates) + Carbonation (CO₂ absorption)
  • Hydration is fast (days)
  • Carbonation slow (weeks/months)
  • Dual-mechanism = faster, stronger set

Properties:

  • Stronger than non-hydraulic lime
  • Sets underwater (due to hydration)
  • Less flexible (more brittle)
  • Can be damp during curing (less sensitive than non-hydraulic)
  • Denser, harder surface

Types (by strength):

Type Silicate Content Strength Uses
Feebly hydraulic Low Moderate Pointing, weakly exposed
Moderately hydraulic Medium Strong Structural mortar, damp areas
Eminently hydraulic High Very strong Underwater, severe exposure

Creating Hydraulic Lime

Natural hydraulic lime:

  • Use limestone with silicate clay content (not pure CaCO₃)
  • Fire at ~900°C (slightly lower than pure limestone)
  • Silicates partially react; hydraulic compounds form

Artificial hydraulic lime (pozzolanic method):

  • Make pure non-hydraulic lime (slake, as above)
  • Add pozzolan (volcanic ash, brick dust, fly ash) to slaked lime
  • Silica reacts slowly with lime
  • Creates hydraulic properties over time

Ratio: 10–20% pozzolan by weight produces useful hydraulic lime

Lime Mortar and Plaster Formulation

Lime Mortar (Non-Hydraulic)

Basic formula:

  • 1 part slaked lime (putty)
  • 2.5–3 parts sand
  • Water to adjust (workable consistency)

Variations:

  • Add filler: Crushed brick, stone dust (improves strength)
  • Add fiber: Hair, straw (reduces cracking)
  • High-quality: Aged putty (years old) produces better mortar

Hydraulic Lime Mortar

Formula:

  • 1 part hydraulic lime
  • 2–2.5 parts sand
  • Water to adjust

Sets faster than non-hydraulic; suitable for pointing and structural work

Lime Plaster

Finish coat (smooth surface):

  • 1 part slaked lime
  • 2–2.5 parts fine sand (or marble dust for white)
  • Fibers (short hair): Reduces checking
  • Optional: Tallow (improves water resistance)

Multiple coats typical:

  • Scratch coat (mechanical key): Coarser
  • Float coat (leveling): Medium
  • Finish coat (cosmetic): Fine sand, smooth troweled

See Interior Finishes guide for detailed plastering technique.

Limewash Application

See Waterproofing and Sealants guide for detailed limewash formulation.

Key points:

  • Thin lime coatings require multiple coats
  • Excellent breathability (prevents moisture trapping)
  • Weathers gracefully (develops patina)
  • Repaints easily
  • Inexpensive

Agricultural Lime Applications

Soil Amendment (Agricultural Lime)

Purpose: Raise soil pH (neutralize acidic soils)

Mechanism:

  • Slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂) is basic (alkaline)
  • Reacts with soil acids; neutralizes
  • Makes soil less acidic; plants grow better in neutral soil

Application rate:

  • Depends on current pH and target pH
  • Typical: 1–5 tons per acre (test soil first)
  • Incorporates into top 6–8 inches

Forms:

  • Ground limestone (slowest; cheap)
  • Hydrated lime (faster; more expensive)
  • Quicklime (fastest, most caustic; requires care)

Effects:

  • Increased microbial activity (alkaline promotes decomposition)
  • Improved nutrient availability (especially phosphorus, molybdenum)
  • Changed soil texture (binds clay; better structure)

Pest and Disease Control

Lime sulfur spray: Lime + sulfur; fungicide/insecticide

  • Controls mites, powdery mildew, aphids
  • Traditional orchard treatment
  • See agricultural guides for details

Whitewash (slaked lime + salt): Protects tree trunks

  • Prevents sunscald (winter sun damage)
  • Deters insects
  • Aesthetic

Lime in Water Treatment

Softening Hard Water

Hard water: Contains dissolved calcium/magnesium

Lime treatment:

  • Slaked lime added to water
  • Ca(OH)₂ reacts with hardness minerals
  • Precipitation: Mineral compounds precipitate out
  • Settling/filtration removes precipitate

Reaction (simplified):

  • Hard water Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺ + OH⁻ (from slaked lime) → CaCO₃ or Mg(OH)₂ precipitate

Result: Softer water; reduced soap scum, mineral deposits

Limitation: Removes only temporary hardness (carbonate); permanent hardness (sulfates, chlorides) remains

Conclusion

Lime is fundamental to construction, agriculture, chemistry, and water treatment. Understanding limestone sources, calcination, slaking, and the difference between hydraulic and non-hydraulic lime enables you to produce and use lime effectively. From traditional mortars to water treatment, lime's versatility has made it essential for millennia and remains vital today.
